::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: The data underlying this article cannot be shared publicly due to GDPR restrictions; it will be shared upon reasonable request to the corresponding author.
Analysis code, full results and supplementary material are available on the OSF (https://osf.io/xj497/overview?view_only=a2b63e3b64874e7980e52c69b381719a).

text.text: Both sleep and stress are important predictors of health and functioning.
Most people would probably agree that sleep and stress are linked: during periods of high stress, one sleeps worse, and after a bad night, one is more easily stressed.
In line with this common perception, previous research has repeatedly shown that stress, particularly in the evening, is linked with poorer sleep, both in quality and quantity [1, 2].
text.formatted: In line with this common perception, previous research has repeatedly shown that stress, particularly in the evening, is linked with poorer sleep, both in quality and quantity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, poor sleep has been linked with increased stress during the next day [2, 3].
text.formatted: Similarly, poor sleep has been linked with increased stress during the next day <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: However, these previous studies had poor temporal resolution regarding both evening and daytime stress, leaving open the question of whether stress at different times of day is differentially associated with sleep.
Furthermore, despite age differences in sleep [4, 5] and stress processes [6, 7], age has thus far received little attention as a moderator of associations between sleep and stress in daily life.
text.formatted: Furthermore, despite age differences in sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref> and stress processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>, age has thus far received little attention as a moderator of associations between sleep and stress in daily life.

text.text: Following the classical transactional model of stress and coping [8] stress arises from an interaction of person and environment through situation-specific appraisals.
text.formatted: Following the classical transactional model of stress and coping <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> stress arises from an interaction of person and environment through situation-specific appraisals.

text.text: That is, a situation does not become "stressful" unless someone perceives their own current resources as insufficient to deal with a potential threat.
Resulting from these appraisals, people experience immediate affective and physiological responses.
As such, studying stress in (near) real time, in people's daily lives using socalled ambulatory assessment designs [9] promises insights into relevant predictors and consequences of momentary stress.
text.formatted: As such, studying stress in (near) real time, in people's daily lives using socalled ambulatory assessment designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> promises insights into relevant predictors and consequences of momentary stress.

text.text: One important such predictor is sleep: Insufficient sleep may reduce (perceived) resources and thus increase perceived stress.

In line with this, ambulatory assessment research has found that both sleeping worse (self-report) and sleeping shorter (self-report and actigraphy) than usual for oneself were linked with higher next-morning expectations of stressors and stressfulness [10].
text.formatted: In line with this, ambulatory assessment research has found that both sleeping worse (self-report) and sleeping shorter (self-report and actigraphy) than usual for oneself were linked with higher next-morning expectations of stressors and stressfulness <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, insufficient sleep may act as a physiological stressor itself [11, 12] and thereby impact psychological stress as well.
text.formatted: Additionally, insufficient sleep may act as a physiological stressor itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref> and thereby impact psychological stress as well.

text.text: Supporting this, findings also extend to physiological and experienced stress.

One study found effects of sleep on self-reported stress and physiological stress markers: Shorter self-reported sleep duration and worse sleep quality were associated with a higher heart rate and higher stress levels that same morning; worse sleep quality was additionally associated with higher blood pressure [13].
text.formatted: One study found effects of sleep on self-reported stress and physiological stress markers: Shorter self-reported sleep duration and worse sleep quality were associated with a higher heart rate and higher stress levels that same morning; worse sleep quality was additionally associated with higher blood pressure <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, several self-reported and actigraphically measured sleep parameters like shorter sleep and lower sleep efficiency were linked with higher subsequent daytime stress in one study [2].
text.formatted: Additionally, several self-reported and actigraphically measured sleep parameters like shorter sleep and lower sleep efficiency were linked with higher subsequent daytime stress in one study <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: This is in contrast to another study in which only self-reported wake after sleep onset, an indicator of sleep fragmentation, was associated with higher severity of reported stressors the next day, whereas EEG-or actigraphy-based sleep parameters were not [3].

text.text: Both self-reported higher sleep quality and longer sleep duration predicted lower odds of reporting stressors the next day [14].

text.text: Previous research has also found that previous stress can predict subsequent sleep in daily life.

One of the earliest daily life studies in this context found that stress and worries at bedtime were the main predictors of sleep quality during the following night; daytime stress only predicted sleep quality in a univariate model, but no longer when bedtime stress and worries were controlled for [1].

text.text: Regarding the mechanisms linking stress to subsequent sleep, research identified pre-sleep arousal as an important within-person mediator of the association between stress and subsequent sleep quality [15, 16].

text.text: Taken together, it seems that stress (remaining) in the evening should be the main predictor of reduced sleep quality and duration, which aligns with research pointing towards the relevance of emotion regulation for sleep, for example, in the context of insomnia [17].

text.text: One important gap in previous research is the poor temporal resolution: With only one to three daily measurements of stress, research has not yet determined whether sleep differentially predicts stress at different times of day.

When looking at other affective outcomes, research has typically found that the effects of sleep on affect are stronger in the morning [18, 19]; thus, it would seem plausible that this could be the case for stress as well.

text.text: The same is true for the opposite direction: While there is substantial evidence that stress and arousal in the evening play an important role for subsequent sleep, little research has considered stress at earlier times throughout the day and earlier or later in the evening.

Based on results from laboratory research [20] and general age differences in sleep and affective functioning [21, 5], it is reasonable to assume people of different ages might differ in effects of sleep on stress and vice versa.

text.text: However, age differences in daily life association between sleep and stress have not received much attention in previous research.

Regarding the effects of sleep on subsequent stress, laboratory research has found that older adults were less vulnerable to cognitive and affective effects of experimentally induced sleep loss [20, 22].

text.text: However, younger and older adults did not differ in reactivity to a standardized laboratorybased stressor following sleep deprivation [12].

text.text: In daily life, younger compared with older adults experienced significantly stronger associations of sleep quality with morning self-rated stress, heart rate, and blood pressure and of sleep duration with heart rate and blood pressure [13].

text.text: Taken together, previous research thus suggests that older adults may be less vulnerable to insufficient sleep and likely react with less of an increase in stress compared with younger adults.
Older adults might experience this reduced vulnerability because they are more used to shorter and low quality sleep [23].
text.formatted: Older adults might experience this reduced vulnerability because they are more used to shorter and low quality sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: In line with this, research has also suggested that older adults may experience a lower homeostatic sleep drive after sleep loss [24].
text.formatted: In line with this, research has also suggested that older adults may experience a lower homeostatic sleep drive after sleep loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, older adults have been suggested to be better able to regulate their emotions [21], which could make potentially threatening situations seem easier to handle.
text.formatted: Additionally, older adults have been suggested to be better able to regulate their emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, which could make potentially threatening situations seem easier to handle.

text.text: At the same time, one of the strengths of older adults' emotion regulation is their ability to avoid potentially stressful situations in the first place [21], that is, they may also particularly avoid stressors after nights with poorer sleep (for a similar argument see [19]).

text.text: Regarding age differences in effects of stress on sleep, there is comparatively less research to build on.

It has been suggested that older adults' sleep may be more vulnerable to the effects of external influences (e.g., caffeine, stress) because they have weaker circadian rhythms, which may be more easily disturbed [25, 26].

text.text: Similarly, older adults may have difficulty down-regulating the physiological arousal associated with increased stress [21, 27] which may also lead to stronger effects of stress on subsequent sleep.

text.text: However, previous research indicated a smaller role of somatic compared with cognitive arousal in explaining the associations of stress with worse subsequent sleep [15, 16] and older adults may be better able to reduce cognitive arousal [21] which could make them less vulnerable.

text.text: Overall, it seems reasonable to assume that younger and older adults may differ in associations of stress with subsequent sleep, but it is difficult to predict the direction of these differences.

text.text: In the current study, we analyze the bidirectional, time-lagged associations of sleep quality and sleep duration with stress assessed up to eight times per day across a 21-day ambulatory assessment study.

Because of the more fine-grained temporal resolution in the measurement of stress, we can overcome limitations of previous research and analyze how sleep is associated with stress at different times of day.
The sample consists of younger and older adults, thus allowing us to consider age differences in the bidirectional associations between sleep and stress.

We hypothesize that poorer sleep, operationalized as shorter sleep duration (actigraphy) and poorer sleep quality (self-rated), is associated with higher self-rated stress the next morning (H1a) and that these associations are less pronounced in older compared with younger adults (H1b).

Similarly, we expect that higher self-rated stress in the evening is associated with poorer subsequent sleep operationalized as shorter actigraphically measured sleep duration and poorer self-rated sleep quality (H2a) and that these associations differ for younger compared with older adults (H2b).
We exploratorily consider sleep efficiency and sleep onset as further sleep parameters.

text.text: Participants included in this study were 161 younger adults (18 -30 years; Mage = 23.8, SD = 3.0, 49.1% male) and 170 older adults (55 -75 years; Mage = 63.6, SD = 5.69, 41.2% male).
Participants were recruited from the larger Stockholm area online forums and social media, as well as paper flyers.
They needed to speak Swedish fluently, own and be able to use a smartphone compatible with the study app PsyMate™, and show no signs of cognitive impairment.

Exclusion criteria included regular shift work and health conditions that may interfere with daily activity, sleep, well-being, and/or cognitive performance (e.g., insomnia, depression, or dementia; for a more detailed description, please refer to the published study protocol [32]).

text.text: Interested participants first answered an online screening survey to determine their eligibility.
Eligible participants then filled out a more extensive online background survey, including questionnaires on, for example, their sleep, health, and well-being.
In the following in-person briefing, participants were screened for cognitive impairment, received further information on the study procedures, and gave written informed consent.
Participants also learned to use the study app PsyMate™ by filling out an exemplary questionnaire, including all questions and the cognitive test.
They further received an actigraph (Motionwatch 8 by CamNtech, Cambridge, United Kingdom) to wear on their non-dominant wrist.
The 21-day ambulatory assessment period started the day after the briefing meeting.

Every participant was called by phone 2-3 days into this phase to ensure everything was working; they also had access to phone support throughout their participation should they encounter any problems.
During the ambulatory assessment period, participants answered up to 10 short questionnaires per day: One morning, one evening and eight daytime questionnaires.

Sleep quality was assessed each morning using four items from the Karolinska Sleep Diary [33].

text.text: Participants reported on problems falling asleep, how calm vs. restless their sleep was, issues with early awakening, and overall perception of sleep quality on a scale of 1 -5, with higher numbers originally indicating worse sleep.
The average across the four items is used as the sleep quality score.

To address our hypotheses and concurrently analyze bidirectional associations between sleep and stress, we used a two-level dynamic structural equation modelling approach in Mplus.
The approach is based on a model that was developed for variables assessed at different time scales, such as sleep and stress in our case [35].

text.text: The model thus considers two levels: Days (Level 1) nested within persons (Level 2).
We used separate models of the same form for each of the sleep variables; in the following we describe the model generally and simply refer to "sleep".
Repeatedly measured variables (sleep, stress) are automatically decomposed into their within-and between-person components (see left part of Figure 2).

text.text: On Level 1, we obtain deviations from people's usual level of sleep and stress.
On Level 2, we obtain a random intercept estimate of the sleep component.

Due to the format of the data, we estimate the random intercept of stress by letting all eight momentary stress variables load onto a common stress factor with a factor loading of 1 to obtain one person-level estimate of stress.
On Level 1, we modelled associations of the previous night's sleep with stress at beeps 1 to 4foot_0 and associations of stress at beeps 4 to 8 with sleep in the next night.

text.text: All these associations are modelled as random slopes, that is, they can differ between participants.

We furthermore included an autoregressive component for sleep (regressing sleep on the previous night's sleep) to account for stability and/or compensatory effects, as well as separate within-day and overnight autoregressive components for stress, because these may be governed by different processes [38, 39].

Similar to the procedure for the random intercept for stress, we estimated one day-time estimate of autoregression per person with all within-day autoregressions loading onto a common factor (day_ar) with a loading of 1 (not depicted in Figure 2 for simplicity).

To determine age differences in associations, we regressed all random effects (intercepts, slopes, residual variances) on a binary age-group variable coding young adults as -0.5 and older adults as 0.5.
This coding scheme has the advantage that model estimates refer to the average across both age groups.
Following the original model [35], we included correlations between all random effects on the between-person level.

The left panel illustrates how each repeatedly measured variable (sleep, momentary stress reports str1-str8) is decomposed into a within-person (Level 1) component (sleep d,i, str1d,i-str8d,i) and a between-person (Level 2) component, i.e., a person-specific random intercept (e.g., sleepi).

The right panel illustrates the structural model.

Level 1 (within-person) models the sequence of momentary stress reports (str1d,i-str8d,i) across a day, linked by autoregressive paths (AR day) and a separate overnight autoregressive path from the last evening beep to the first beep of the next day (AR night).
Sleepd,i predicts stress at the first four beeps of the following day (paths b_1str-b_4str), and stress at beeps 4-8 predicts sleepd+1,i on the subsequent night (paths b_4sleep-b_8sleep).
Sleep also has an autoregressive component linking sleep from one night to the next (AR sleep).

Level 2 includes between-person components of all parameters: the random intercepts (sleepi, stri), the autoregressive parameters (AR dayi, AR nighti, AR sleepi), and the random slopes for the sleep-stress associations (b_1stri-b_4stri, b_4sleepi-b_8sleepi).
All of these random effects are regressed on age group (young vs. older adults, coded -0.5/0.5) and correlate with one another.
This model was fitted for self-reported sleep quality and actigraphically measured sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and sleep onset separately.
As preregistered, a significant association of previous sleep with stress at beep 1 and/or beep 2 would support hypothesis H1a regarding insufficient sleep predicting stronger stress in the morning.

Deviating from the preregistration, we decided to include associations of sleep with subsequent stress not only at the first two but rather at the first four beeps as a more severe test of our hypothesis that sleep should predict stress specifically in the morning.
Thus, sleep predicting stress at beep 3 or 4 (as well) would speak against H1a.
This procedure mirrors the preregistered analysis and decision rules for hypothesis H2a regarding stress in the evening predicting subsequent sleep.
Here, a significant association of stress at beeps 7 and/or 8 with subsequent sleep would support H2a whereas any significant associations of stress at earlier beeps would speak against it.
Significant age group differences in associations of sleep with stress or stress with subsequent sleep would support H1b and H2b respectively.

text.text: When combining stress reported at beeps 7 and 8, higher stress reported at people's last beep before going to bed predicted lower sleep quality, but not shorter or longer sleep duration.
However, higher stress at beep 6 predicted shorter sleep duration.
To situate the unexpected association of higher stress at beep 8 with longer sleep duration in the main model, we ran further analyses.

First, to assess multicollinearity as one potential explanation, we calculated a variance inflation factor (VIF) for the within-person parts of stress at beeps 4 to 8 (i.e., the predictors of sleep the following night).
With VIF = 1.13, multicollinearity does not seem to be a major issue.
Another explanation could be suppression effects, that is, effects of one predictor variable changing because of shared variance with another predictor being "suppressed".
To see results without this potential suppression, we repeated the analyses using only stress at beep 8 or only stress at beep 7 as predictors.
In these analyses, stress at beep 8 no longer predicted longer sleep duration, and stress at beep 7 predicted shorter sleep as before.
Both lower stress at beep 8 and stress at beep 7 predicted better sleep quality in these models.
The relevant parameters from these analyses are reported in the supplement (Table S4).

text.text: There was only one significant age difference in associations of stress with subsequent sleep:
The association of stress at beep 6 with sleep quality was significantly more positive for older compared with younger adults.
Simple slope analyses showed that older adults experienced better sleep quality with higher stress at beep 6 (p = .019), whereas younger adults did not (p = .266).
This effect was not significant in the model where we combined the stress at beep 7 and beep 8 to only include the last report before going to bed.
We additionally analyzed associations of sleep efficiency and sleep onset time with subsequent stress.
Whereas sleep efficiency did not predict stress the next day, later sleep onset was associated with lower stress throughout the first half of the day.

In models controlling for weekends/holidays, naps, subjective health, BMI and full-time retirement, higher sleep efficiency predicted lower stress at beep 1 and beep 4 in these models, which it did not previously.
In contrast, later sleep onset was no longer associated with lower stress when controlling for these variables.
However, a significant age difference emerged: The association of later sleep onset with stress at beep 2 was significantly more positive in older compared with younger adults.
Simple slopes analyses indicated that later sleep onset was associated with higher stress at beep two for older (p = .010) but not for younger adults (p = .067).
For the opposite direction, higher stress at beep 8 predicted higher sleep efficiency, whereas higher stress at beep 6 predicted lower sleep efficiency.
Higher stress at beep 5 again predicted higher sleep efficiency.
Stress did not predict sleep onset time.
These results remained in the models, including control variables.
Results for these models are reported in the Supplement (Table S5).

text.text: In the models, we see age-related differences in stress, with older adults reporting lower stress on average.
Regarding sleep, we see a difference in sleep onset, with older adults sleeping earlier compared to younger adults.
There were no significant age-group differences in sleep quality, sleep duration, or sleep efficiency in the unadjusted models.

In the adjusted models, controlling for weekends/holidays, naps, subjective health, BMI and full-time retirement, we additionally observed an age difference in sleep quality, with lower sleep quality for older adults.

We observed substantial stress inertia, i.e., previous stress predicting subsequent stress, both within-days and overnight: Within-day stress inertia was 0.358, 95% CI = [0.336, 0.380] and overnight stress inertia 0.190, 95% CI = [0.130, 0.248].

These effects differed by age group: Inertia was stronger for younger compared with older adults, both within-day (b = -0.214, 95% CI = [-0.331, -0.088]) and overnight (b = -0.198, 95% CI = [-0.350, -0.040]).
At the between-person level, people who experienced better sleep quality also reported lower stress on average (r = -0.333, 95% CI = [-0.441, -0.216]).

There were no significant associations of average sleep duration (r = -0.007, 95% CI = [-0.127, 0.115]), sleep onset (r = -0.004, 95% CI = [-0.122, 0.129]), or sleep efficiency (r = -0.011, 95% CI = [-0.111, 0.132]) with average stress.
2 The reported numerical results are from the unadjusted model including sleep quality.
Taken together, when people reported lower quality sleep than usual for them, they experienced higher stress throughout the first half of the following day.
With shorter sleep duration, people mainly experienced higher stress early in the morning but also around midday.
Both of these findings are in contrast to the hypothesis (H1a) that sleep quality should mainly be linked specifically with stress in the morning.

For the opposite direction, when people experienced higher than usual stress at beep 8 (time interval 21:00-23:00) or the last beep they answered in the evening (combined beep 7/8, time interval 19:00-23:00) they reported lower sleep quality for the following night, supporting hypothesis H2a for sleep quality.
Findings regarding associations of stress with sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and sleep onset differed depending on modelling choices.
In contrast to hypotheses H1b and H2b, there were hardly any age differences in associations between sleep and stress.

Generally aligning with previous research, we observed effects of previous higher quality and longer sleep with lower stress throughout the first half of the day (7:00-15:00), not only during morning hours.

For sleep quality, we found this effect consistently across all included beeps 1 to 4; for sleep duration, some effects were more stable than others: Shorter sleep duration only consistently predicted higher stress at beeps 1 and 3.

Given that effects of sleep on stress persisted past the morning into the early afternoon, future research my consider analysing whether effects further extend into the late afternoon and evening as well.

The findings generally support the theoretical supposition and results from sleep deprivation studies showing that lower quality and shorter duration sleep may increase stress, for example through reduced available resources and increased activity in physiological stress systems [12, 40].

text.text: Similar to previous findings regarding affect [19, 18], these associations appeared numerically strongest in the morning and weaker for stress later in the day, although we did not test whether this difference was statistically significant.
text.formatted: Similar to previous findings regarding affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>, these associations appeared numerically strongest in the morning and weaker for stress later in the day, although we did not test whether this difference was statistically significant.

text.text: In contrast to most previous research, we included autoregressive paths for stress, thus an effect of sleep on stress at beep 2 reflects the association with stress at beep 2 above and beyond higher levels of stress carrying-over from beep 1.
Accordingly, the effects of sleep quality on subsequent stress seem to play out across several hours, not just in the (early) morning.
Other research has indicated that lower quality sleep may further be associated with increased affective inertia [39].
text.formatted: Other research has indicated that lower quality sleep may further be associated with increased affective inertia <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: We observed substantial inertia in feeling stressed, and it is possible that sleep quality, duration, or other sleep parameters might be linked with stress inertia, i.e., reduced recovery from stress.
This association cannot be tested with the current model but would be an interesting question for future research to consider.
Surprisingly, later sleep onset was associated with lower stress at beeps 1 -4, however these associations were no longer significant in the models including control variables such as weekend.

One plausible explanation for this finding would thus be that people both went to bed later and experienced less stress on the weekend compared with weekdays, which aligns with the observed zero-order correlations.
In this study, we only observed significant associations of sleep efficiency with subsequent stress in the model with control variables.
Given that sleep efficiency was linked with subsequent stress in previous research [2], future research may explore potential boundary conditions for this association.
text.formatted: Given that sleep efficiency was linked with subsequent stress in previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, future research may explore potential boundary conditions for this association.

text.text: In contrast to our hypotheses, we did not consistently observe effects of stress in the (late) evening on subsequent sleep across different sleep parameters.
Rather, effects were more nuanced.

Whereas theoretically predicted findings regarding increased stress before going to bed predicting impaired subsequent sleep quality largely held and stress earlier in the day did not play a role here, this was not true for sleep duration.
More stress at beep 8 instead predicted longer sleep duration, but higher stress earlier in the day mostly predicted shorter sleep (beep 7, 19:00-21:00, and beep 4, 13:00-15:00).
The results for sleep quality support our hypothesis and are in line with previous research showing that higher stress in the evening is linked with lower subsequent sleep quality [1].
text.formatted: The results for sleep quality support our hypothesis and are in line with previous research showing that higher stress in the evening is linked with lower subsequent sleep quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The findings partially showing links of higher stress with longer sleep are rather puzzling, as most research so far has observed that, if anything, higher stress in the evening predicted shorter subsequent sleep [2, 3].
text.formatted: The findings partially showing links of higher stress with longer sleep are rather puzzling, as most research so far has observed that, if anything, higher stress in the evening predicted shorter subsequent sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: However, none of the previous research had the same level of temporal resolution and considered stress across the afternoon and evening as separate predictors of sleep.
To further situate this unexpected finding, we thus consider results from additional analyses.

Firstly, in the pre-registered sensitivity analyses combining stress reports from beep 7 and beep 8, the last stress report before people went to bed was no longer associated with longer or more efficient sleep.

In additional analyses, only including stress at beep 8 or stress at beep 7 and not any other beeps, higher stress was not associated with longer subsequent sleep duration either, rather, higher stress at beep 7 predicted shorter sleep.
Jointly considering these findings suggests that there may have been a suppressor effect at play.
That is, the observed effects of stress at beep 8 may have resulted from shared variance with stress at another time (most likely beep 7) being "suppressed".

Alternatively, it is also possible that this effect could simply be the result of a type-1 error, considering the overall number of tests as well as how close the lower end of the reported CI is to zero.
Accordingly, we refrain from overinterpreting this effect here.
Regarding the expected but not observed effects of increased stress on shorter sleep duration, one further aspect to consider is delayed sleep onset as a potential mechanism.
However, in this study, stress across the afternoon and evening was not associated with delayed sleep onset either.
In the following, we consider some characteristics of the stress measurements that could help in interpreting the overall findings.

First of all, participants in this study reported low levels of stress on average (between 3.27-3.80 on a 9-point scale, i.e., well below the scale mid-point of5 = neither relaxed nor stressed), with the lowest average stress ratings occurring in the evening.

Furthermore, the effects of stress on subsequent sleep were at least partially mediated through cognitive pre-sleep arousal in previous research [41, 15, 16] and an increased rating on the applied stress-scale, especially on the lower end of the scale, may not necessarily imply increased cognitive arousal.
text.formatted: Furthermore, the effects of stress on subsequent sleep were at least partially mediated through cognitive pre-sleep arousal in previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref> and an increased rating on the applied stress-scale, especially on the lower end of the scale, may not necessarily imply increased cognitive arousal.

text.text: Instead of linear effects of within-person deviations, it is possible that stress only impacts subsequent sleep once it crosses a certain threshold.
However, in the current study high stress ratings were rare: only 5.9% of cases used the ratings 7 (=stressed) or higher on the 9-point scale.

These findings thus highlight the need to more closely consider and model the potentially non-linear mechanisms through which stress at different times of day may differentially impair different aspects of sleep at night.
In contrast to our hypotheses, younger and older adults did not generally differ in associations between sleep and stress.
Normal variations in sleep, as they occur in daily life, were overall not differentially linked with self-reported stress for younger and older adults.

This is in contrast to lab-based findings on affective functioning, which found that older adults were less vulnerable to affective consequences of sleep loss [20] and initial findings from daily life more strongly linking sleep quality with self-reported and physiological stress in the morning for younger compared with older adults [13].
text.formatted: This is in contrast to lab-based findings on affective functioning, which found that older adults were less vulnerable to affective consequences of sleep loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> and initial findings from daily life more strongly linking sleep quality with self-reported and physiological stress in the morning for younger compared with older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: However, the findings align with previous research showing similar stress responses to a standardized stressor in the laboratory following sleep loss (TSST) [12].
text.formatted: However, the findings align with previous research showing similar stress responses to a standardized stressor in the laboratory following sleep loss (TSST) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, shorter sleep duration predicted higher stress at beep 2 specifically for older but not younger adults.
Because this effect disappeared in the adjusted model, it is possible that it may have been driven by the fully retired older adults, however, this is merely speculative.
No comparable effects were found in the models combining stress at beep 1 and 2 to reflect the first stress report in the morning.
For the opposite direction, more stress at beep 6 was linked with better sleep quality the next night for older but not for younger adults, both in models with and without control variables.

Considering the generally low levels of stress reported in the study, even more so by older adults, slightly increased stress in the late afternoon may imply increased activity more than actual stress, which might be linked with better sleep quality.
Previous research has also found quadratic associations of stress reactivity with health and well-being [42], suggesting that some level of reacting to stress may generally be adaptive.

text.text: In light of age differences within old age in previous research (e.g., [19]), it is important to consider that this study includes a rather heterogeneous older sample: Strictly speaking, part of the sample would still be considered middle-aged, and some people were still working, whereas others were fully retired.
text.formatted: In light of age differences within old age in previous research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>), it is important to consider that this study includes a rather heterogeneous older sample: Strictly speaking, part of the sample would still be considered middle-aged, and some people were still working, whereas others were fully retired.

text.text: Accordingly, grouping together this heterogeneous group may have overshadowed potential effects.

Furthermore, very old adults in the (> 80 years) who generally experience stronger declines in functioning may differ from late middle-aged and "young-old" adults [43] and might become more vulnerable to stress-effects on sleep, which should be considered in future research.

text.text: This research has several important strengths, namely, a large age-heterogeneous sample (N = 331), a long assessment period with many data points (21 days with an average of 116 data points per person compared to the average of 12.4 days with 51 data points per person in a meta-analysis of ambulatory assessment studies [44]), and high temporal resolution with up to eight daily reports of stress.
text.formatted: This research has several important strengths, namely, a large age-heterogeneous sample (N = 331), a long assessment period with many data points (21 days with an average of 116 data points per person compared to the average of 12.4 days with 51 data points per person in a meta-analysis of ambulatory assessment studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>), and high temporal resolution with up to eight daily reports of stress.

text.text: To make best use of this high temporal resolution, we applied a model specifically designed to study dynamics of variables assessed at different time scales [38], which allowed us to assess differential associations of sleep with stress at different times of the day.
text.formatted: To make best use of this high temporal resolution, we applied a model specifically designed to study dynamics of variables assessed at different time scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>, which allowed us to assess differential associations of sleep with stress at different times of the day.

text.text: This measurement and modelling approach is also an important point to consider when comparing results of the current study with those of previous studies.
Including several correlated measures of stress across the second part of the day as predictors of subsequent sleep, we may have inadvertently reduced power for each separate one of those effects.

Future research may consider testing how different "configurations" of stress throughout the afternoon predict subsequent sleep, for example, average stress, the amount and/or timing of the strongest experience of stress, recovery trajectories or similar.
Furthermore, the meaning of "feeling stressed" may not be invariant across persons or time:
In line with previous research, we assessed stress rather broadly by asking people how stressed they currently felt.
As such, we do not know how people defined feeling relaxed vs. stressed at different times.
It is possible that something that would not have increased their stress ratings during waking hours could be counted as more stressful late at night.

Supporting this general idea, recent qualitative research showed that people's interpretation of ambulatory assessment items varies over time and that they consider different aspects of their recent experiences when answering these items [45].
text.formatted: Supporting this general idea, recent qualitative research showed that people's interpretation of ambulatory assessment items varies over time and that they consider different aspects of their recent experiences when answering these items <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref>.

text.text: More qualitative assessments of stress would enable new insights into people's reasons for feeling stressed (e.g., the type of stressor) and could be included in future research on links between sleep and stress.
Similarly, when we consider stress as a process, we can differentiate phases such as anticipation, reactivity, or recovery [46], which might be differently associated with sleep [19, 47].
text.formatted: Similarly, when we consider stress as a process, we can differentiate phases such as anticipation, reactivity, or recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>, which might be differently associated with sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47]</ref>.

text.text: This paper focused on within-person associations between sleep and stress -however, it is possible that between-person differences in stress or sleep may impact within-person associations.
For example, one could imagine people who are chronically stressed also sleep poorly in general but no longer react to (minor) changes in stress from day to day.
This may be an important consideration for future research. predicted lower sleep duration and efficiency.

text.text: Applying a state-of-the-art dynamic structural equation model designed to analyze dynamic associations of variables assessed on different time scales, the effects of previous sleep on subsequent stress were more consistent than those of stress on subsequent sleep.
This is in line with most previous research using simpler models.

Extending and adding specificity to previous findings, we found that lower quality sleep not only predicted stress in the morning but also throughout the first half of the day, even after controlling for stress at earlier times.
Future research may consider assessing effects of sleep on stress throughout the second half of the day as well.
